history.title:
PLAZA
DE MAYO
history.body:
The square is bounded by Rivadavia, Bolívar, Hipólito Yrigoyen and Balcarce, and three avenues leave its west side: Avenida de Mayo and the two diagonals. The arcade of the old Recova that once crossed it was pulled down in 1883, and the modern square was laid out the next year. Round it stand the Casa Rosada, the Cabildo, the Catedral, the Palacio Municipal and the Banco de la Nación; under it run the subte's Plaza de Mayo, Catedral and Bolívar stations.

The Casa Rosada is pink, and nobody agrees why: some say Sarmiento chose it to mix the Federalists' red with the Unitarians' white, others that the paint was mixed with cow's blood against the damp. Tamburini's central arch, finished in 1898, joined two older buildings into one.
history.foot: The night of the snow is made up. The square is not.

history.title:
THE
PIRÁMIDE
history.body:
The Pirámide de Mayo is the oldest monument in the city, raised in 1811 for the first anniversary of the May Revolution. Prilidiano Pueyrredón rebuilt it larger in 1856 over the old core, with the national arms on all four sides of its base. It is 18.76 metres to the tip of the cap of its Liberty, who is 3.6 metres tall. A golden sun faces the Casa Rosada; laurel crowns are on the other three faces.

In November 1912 it was moved some 63 metres east, on rails, to the middle of the square. Its four corner statues were taken away that year and only came back in 2018, so in 1958 it stood without them. The eight Canary palms round it were planted between 1900 and 1904.
history.foot: In 1958 the Pirámide had no statues at its corners.

history.title:
THE
CABILDO
history.body:
The Cabildo was the town hall of colonial Buenos Aires, and the May Revolution of 1810 was argued under its roof. The city kept cutting it back: three of its northern arches went in 1889 to open Avenida de Mayo, and its tall tower with them; three more went from the south end in 1931. Only five of the original arches were left.

In 1939 and 1940 the architect Mario Buschiazzo restored what remained: the tower was rebuilt, the red colonial roof tiles put back, with iron bars on the windows and wooden doors and shutters made after the old ones. The Cabildo of 1958, with its five arches, is that one.
history.foot: The arcade's fuse box is made up.

history.title:
THE
SUBTE
history.body:
The first underground railway in Latin America, and in the southern hemisphere, opened under Avenida de Mayo on 1 December 1913, from Plaza de Mayo to Plaza Miserere. It was the Anglo-Argentina's Línea A, and its wooden cars ran for nearly a hundred years. Its first station lies under the head of the avenue, at the square.

The trams that ran on Rivadavia in 1958 were nearly at their end: the network was renewed between 1955 and 1961, and then broken up. The last trams in the city ran in February 1963.
history.foot: The service stair at the corner of the square is made up.

history.title:
THE
SNOW
history.body:
Snow almost never falls on Buenos Aires. On 22 June 1918 it began in the afternoon and came again, heavier, at night; people poured out to see it, and there were crowds in the Plaza de Mayo, a snowball fight in the Plaza del Congreso, shop clerks out on the pavements. A photograph of that day shows the Plaza de Mayo white. Six people died of the cold, among them people sleeping in the street.

It snowed again on 9 July 2007, for the first time in 89 years, and again whole families went out to watch it fall. No snow fell in 1958.
history.foot: This snow is not that snow.

history.title:
THE
COMIC
history.body:
The comic by Héctor Germán Oesterheld and Francisco Solano López, which began to appear in Hora Cero Semanal in 1957, on 4 September, brings down on Buenos Aires a luminous snow that kills whatever it touches, and a handful of neighbours band together to live through it. It ran in 106 weekly instalments into 1959: on a winter night in 1958 it was at the kiosks.

This prologue borrows its snowfall for one night in the Plaza de Mayo and, with its rights holders' permission, its Juan Salvo and its cascarudos. The four neighbours from La Boca and everyone in the square are the game's own.
history.foot: A private preview, made to be shown to the comic's rights holders.

copy.title:
PLAZA
DE MAYO
copy.briefing:
Buenos Aires, a winter night in 1958, and for the first time in forty years it is snowing. Half the city has come to the Plaza de Mayo to see it. Within minutes the ones who stay out in it begin to fall: the snow kills whoever it touches. Four neighbours from La Boca happened to be under cover when it began: Hornero at the controls of a tram stopped on Rivadavia, Lechuza under the Cabildo's arcade, Benteveo selling the Sexta on the Catedral's steps, Biguá on a colectivo stranded on Hipólito Yrigoyen.

Early in the night Juan Salvo comes in off Avenida de Mayo, sealed in an insulating suit: the snow cannot touch him, he can carry in whoever has fallen, and he has a rifle with a few rounds. Soon the cascarudos come up the avenues, each as big as a car, and knock down whoever they find out in the open. They will not go under the arches or the portico, down into the subte or into the tram, and noise draws them. Bring in as many as you can before the snow buries the square. Watch the waves; move in the lulls.
copy.debrief: By midnight the square was a field of snow, and the Pirámide stood up out of it like a post in a river. Nobody came out from under the arches that night, or down from the tram. In the subte they listened to the snow through the gratings and waited for the morning, and the five of them counted heads.
copy.failureNote: Lose the whole squad, or bring in too few before the snow buries the square, and it is over. Watch the snow: move in the lulls, wait out the waves under cover, and stop the clock to give orders.
copy.checkpointNote: Checkpoints are also taken when Juan Salvo comes, when the arcade's lights come on and when the service gate opens.

howto.line: Tap Hornero, Lechuza, Benteveo or Biguá to choose who acts, then tap a person out in the snow: they follow him. Lead them under cover: the portico, the arcade, the subte, the tram, the colectivo.
The ring over each head is the cold. It fills out in the snow, faster in a wave, and empties under cover. Full, they fall: Biguá or Juan Salvo can still carry them in.
The snow comes in waves. Wait out the heavy ones under cover and cross in the lulls. PLAN stops the clock: give each an order, then EXECUTE.
Benteveo's shout gathers everyone near him behind him. Hornero's bell, rung from the tram, brings people running to it.

Hornero drives the tram along Rivadavia and Biguá the colectivo along Yrigoyen. Everyone aboard goes with them: cover on wheels. The three at the Balcarce stop cannot walk: bring the colectivo to them.
Cascarudos come up the avenues for whoever is out in the open, and noise draws them. Juan Salvo's rifle drives them off; the rifle in the sentry box arms one more of you.
A cloth keeps the snow off a few for one crossing. The hood and mask by the truck on Yrigoyen seal one of you against it for the whole night.
